svg.title: The BGP best-path decision process as an ordered sequence, with criterion eight highlighted
svg.desc: Twelve criteria evaluated in order, stopping at the first difference. One, highest weight, local to the router and never advertised. Two, highest local preference, shared inside the autonomous system. Three, locally originated, either a network command or a redistribute. Four, shortest AS_PATH. Five, lowest origin code, where IGP beats EGP beats incomplete. Six, lowest multi-exit discriminator. Seven, external over internal, then internal over confederation-external. Eight, lowest IGP metric to the next hop, which is the criterion that silently decides many enterprise designs. Nine, oldest route for external BGP. Ten, lowest router ID of the advertising neighbour. Eleven, shortest cluster list. Twelve, lowest neighbour address. Criterion eight is highlighted with a note explaining that criteria one to seven can all tie and then an IGP cost nobody chose becomes the winner. A side note lists three facts that are commonly wrong: weight is local and never leaves the router, MED is only compared between paths from the same neighbouring autonomous system by default, and a route not installed may fail because its next hop is unreachable rather than because of a policy.
svg.text: Best path: compare in order, stop at the first difference — there is no scoring and no averaging
Read the list as a tie-breaker chain; most real disagreements are settled by items 1 to 8
Weight (highest, local only) → Local preference (highest, whole AS) → locally originated
The three you control directly. If a design “does not work”, check these first — they consume no IGP knowledge and no convergence.
Shortest AS_PATH → lowest origin (IGP < EGP < incomplete) → lowest MED
The inter-domain set. MED only compares paths from the same neighbouring AS, so it is a hint, not a decision.
eBGP over iBGP over confederation-external
This is why an external path with a worse AS_PATH can still beat a cleaner internal one: the origin class outranks the path length here.
Lowest IGP metric to the NEXT_HOP
Items 1–7 can all tie. Then an IGP cost that nobody designed for BGP decides the path, and it is the
sum of interface costs that came from a bandwidth formula. Design the IGP cost and the BGP policy together.
Oldest eBGP route → lowest router ID of the advertising neighbour
Tie-breakers with no design meaning. If you reach them, the policy above was not specific enough.
Shortest cluster list → lowest neighbour address
Which is effectively the router's own address book deciding. Document it if it ever shows up in a post-mortem.
THREE THINGS PEOPLE GET WRONG
Weight is local
It is never advertised and never received. A weight set
on one router is invisible to its peers, so “we set weight
everywhere” often means “on the router I logged into”.
Use local preference when the intent is network-wide.
MED is not an absolute
By default it is compared only between paths from the
same neighbouring AS. Setting MED 50 towards one ISP
and 100 towards another compares nothing at all.
It is a suggestion inside one business relationship.
Best path is not installed path
A route can win the comparison and still not reach the
FIB, because its NEXT_HOP is unreachable through the
IGP. That is a recursive lookup failure, not a policy bug.
Check next-hop reachability before editing attributes.
How to use this list in operations: when two paths disagree with the intent, walk down the list with the actual output in hand until the first item
that differs. That item is the answer — not the attribute you assumed was in charge. Writing the item number in the ticket turns a debate
into a fact, and it is the fastest way to find a policy that was applied in the wrong direction.
